title: Finding Just the Right Analogy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case for analogy as a core persuasive tool for leaders trying to make new or abstract ideas land quickly with an audience. It explains the mechanics of a good analogy — a comparison that maps a familiar, well-understood concept onto an unfamiliar one so listeners can transfer their existing understanding — and warns against reaching for tired, overused comparisons. The piece offers a practical search method: identify which features of an idea are hardest to grasp, then look for familiar objects, processes, or events that share those specific features. It closes by noting that strong analogies become reusable 'old friends' that a leader can invoke repeatedly to reinforce understanding.
points: The essay defines analogy precisely as a comparison built on shared specific features, not just a loose or decorative metaphor.
It offers a concrete search heuristic for building analogies: identify the hardest-to-grasp features of an idea first, then hunt for familiar objects or events sharing those exact features.
It explicitly warns against overused comparisons (time as a river, the brain as a computer), pushing leaders toward more creative and memorable options.
The framing of a good analogy as an 'old friend' that can be reused repeatedly gives it a longer-term communication value beyond a single presentation.
quotes: Good leaders rely heavily on analogies to explain their ideas, proposals, and concepts. They understand that a great analogy conveys an abstract idea in a highly relatable way.
This comparison helps to break down the complexity of the idea by giving others something they know how to latch onto.
The key is to find analogies that are not tired and overused. We all know that time is like a river, a brain is like a computer, life is like a rollercoaster.
By drawing parallels to concrete and familiar concepts, leaders use analogies to paint a picture that makes complex ideas more understandable.
Great analogies become “old friends” quickly and can be repeated again and again to aid understanding.
